content.text: Skills, MCP servers, subagents, hooks and plugins aren't five ways to do the same thing. Each one changes a different part of Claude Code: what Claude knows, what it can reach, where the work runs, what always happens, and how the setup travels. Pick by the question you're answering, and expect a real setup to combine several.
A team wants Claude to triage bug tickets the way their on-call engineer does, so one developer writes a single
/triage
skill. It holds everything: a
curl

command with the error tracker's API token pasted in, "read every file in logs/ until you find the request", the triage playbook, and "ALWAYS run the regression suite before you finish!!!". It half works. The token gets committed with
.claude/skills/

. The log reads fill the conversation until it compacts. Claude skips the regression suite on days it decides a fix is trivial. And when a second team wants the same thing, they copy the folder and the two versions drift apart.
The common misconception
"Skills, MCP, subagents, hooks and plugins are all ways to give Claude a new capability, so use whichever one you know." It's an easy conclusion to reach:

items.text: They really do overlap. A skill can run in a subagent, a subagent can preload skills, a hook can call an MCP tool, and a plugin can contain all of them.
A skill can run shell commands, so it looks like it could stand in for an MCP server or a hook.
They all live as files under
.claude/
or in settings, and several show up in the same
menu.
Installing a plugin adds skills, agents, hooks and servers in one step, so "plugin" sounds like a capability itself.

content.text: The half-truth is the overlap. They compose well, but they aren't interchangeable: each one plugs into a different point in Claude's loop, and they differ in who triggers them and what they cost.
What actually happens
Five questions, five answers
The docs' overview of extensions boils down to one question per feature:

items.text: What should Claude know, or how should it do a task?
A
skill
: a
SKILL.md
file of instructions or reference material. The docs call skills "the most flexible extension".
What can Claude reach?
An
MCP
server: tools for an external system, "with the connection and authentication handled by the server". The docs' trigger: you keep copying data into chat from another tool.
Where should the work happen?
A
subagent
: its own context window and instructions. It can read dozens of files, and your conversation receives only its summary.
What must happen every time?
A
hook
: Claude Code runs it at a lifecycle event, such as after every edit, without Claude deciding.
How does this reach another repo or team?
A
plugin
: the packaging layer. It bundles skills, agents, hooks and MCP servers into one installable unit.

content.text: Who pulls the trigger
This is the difference that matters most. You or Claude starts a skill: you type
/name

, or Claude matches its description to your task. Claude decides when to call an MCP tool or delegate to a subagent. Nobody decides when a hook runs; its event fires and Claude Code runs it. That's why "always run the regression suite" fails inside a skill: a skill is instructions Claude interprets, and the docs say plainly that its outcome can vary.
What each one costs in context
Most extensions take some context, and too much adds noise as well as cost. They load very differently:

rows.text: The description every request; the body once used
Claude, when it calls a tool
Tool names at start; full schemas only on demand
Data and actions in an external system
Its description; the work runs in its own window
Side tasks that read a lot and return a little
Nothing, unless the hook returns output
Its components' costs, in every session it's enabled
Sharing one setup across repos and teams

content.text: The triage skill, split up
Here is the skill before and after each job moves to the extension built for it:

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
---
description: Triage a bug ticket
---
1. Fetch the error:
   curl -H "Authorization: Bearer sntrys_EXAMPLE" \
     "https://errors.example.com/api/issues/$ARGUMENTS/latest"
2. Read every file in logs/ until you find the request.
3. Find the root cause and fix it.
4. ALWAYS run pnpm test:regression before you finish!!!

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
---
description: Triage a bug ticket from its error-tracker issue.
  Use when the user shares a ticket ID or an issue link.
---
1. Get the issue and its latest event with the tracker's MCP tools.
2. Hand the log search to the log-digger subagent. Ask it for the
   failing request and its trace ID, nothing else.
3. Write the root cause, the fix and how you checked it.

content.text: Each line of the old skill went somewhere specific. The
curl

call and its token became an MCP server, which handles the connection; the credential comes from an OAuth sign-in or an environment variable, not a committed file. The log search became a subagent, so forty log files no longer pass through the main conversation. The ALWAYS line became a
Stop
hook that runs the regression suite whenever Claude tries to finish. What's left in the skill is what only a skill does well: the judgment steps.
When the second team asks for it, all four pieces ship as one plugin:

blocks.code:
triage-kit/
├── .claude-plugin/plugin.json   # manifest: the name "triage-kit"
├── skills/triage/SKILL.md       # the playbook: /triage-kit:triage
├── agents/log-digger.md         # subagent: searches logs, returns a summary
├── hooks/hooks.json             # Stop hook: runs the regression suite
└── .mcp.json                    # the error tracker's MCP server

content.text: Plugin skills are namespaced, so the command becomes
/triage-kit:triage
and can't collide with a team's own
/triage
. Both teams now update one plugin instead of two copies.

blocks.title: Follow the triggers, not the feature list

content.text: You don't need all five on day one. The docs list a trigger for each: Claude gets a convention wrong twice (CLAUDE.md), you paste the same playbook a third time (skill), you keep copying data from a browser tab (MCP), a side task floods the conversation (subagent), something must happen without asking (hook), a second repo needs the same setup (plugin).

blocks.title: An enabled plugin is in every session

content.text: A plugin isn't free when you're not using it. The name and description of each skill and agent Claude can invoke sit in context on every turn, its MCP servers run alongside each session, and its hooks fire at their events. Check the footprint before installing, and disable plugins you're not using with
/plugin

blocks.title: Plugins and MCP servers run as you

content.text: The docs are blunt: "what the plugin runs, it runs as you", whatever marketplace it came from. Even most of what Anthropic's official marketplace lists comes from partners and other authors, and a plugin from a third-party marketplace, a coworker's repo or a skills collection is community, not official. Read what it runs before installing, and verify you trust each MCP server: one that fetches external content can expose you to prompt injection.
How to apply it in your project
Run
/hooks
/mcp
and
/plugin
to see what's configured, and
/context
to see what it costs.

items.title: Ask the five questions of each piece

content.text: Knowledge, reach, isolation, guarantee or packaging? A skill that does two of those is two things.
Credentials belong in an MCP server's configuration, at local scope if they shouldn't be committed.
A skill line that must hold every time becomes a hook, and the skill keeps the steps that need judgment.
Skills, subagents, hooks and MCP servers all work without a plugin. Build one when a second repo or team needs the setup.
Key takeaways

items.text: A skill changes what Claude knows or how it works; Claude or you decide when it loads.
An MCP server changes what Claude can reach, with auth handled by the server.
A subagent changes where the work happens; only its summary comes back.
A hook changes what always happens, because Claude Code runs it on an event.
A plugin changes nothing on its own: it ships the other four, and it costs context in every session it's enabled.
